content: Wheatgrass is a young plant belonging to the genus Caroline, particularly Agropyron cristatum, which is a relative of wheat. Some wheatgrass products are also derived from Triticum aestivum, commonly known as common wheat. The fresh leaf buds of wheatgrass can be juiced or dried into a powder, both of which provide a variety of nutrients, including chlorophyll, amino acids, minerals, vitamins, and enzymes. The unprocessed plant also contains dietary fiber, which is beneficial for maintaining colon health. The use of wheatgrass in Western countries began in the 1930s, largely due to the efforts of Charles F. Schnabel, who sought to popularize the plant. In the 1940s, Ann Wigmore further contributed to its popularity, claiming that wheatgrass played a role in the remission of her cancer. Wigmore authored several books on the subject, promoting its health benefits. The typical dosage of wheatgrass consumed by individuals is around 3 to 5 grams, either in powder or tablet form. Some people prefer to consume a freshly squeezed 30 mL shot daily, while others seeking therapeutic benefits may take higher doses of 2 to 4 ounces, one to three times per day, on an empty stomach and before meals. For detoxification purposes, some users increase their intake to three to four times per day. However, individuals with poor dietary habits may experience nausea when consuming high doses of wheatgrass. Wheatgrass grown indoors under artificial conditions is less nutrient-dense compared to wheatgrass grown outdoors in natural environments. Freshly squeezed wheatgrass juice is particularly low in nutrients, as it is composed of 95% water and only 5% dry matter, unlike its dehydrated counterparts. Outdoor wheatgrass, grown in regions known for winter wheat, such as the breadbasket areas of the United States and Canada, is only available for a few days each year. Winter wheat requires over 200 days of slow growth in cold temperatures to achieve peak nutritional content. Even after this extended growth period, the plant remains only 7 to 10 inches tall, as it grows naturally during the cold winter months in climates like the Midwestern United States. In contrast, tray-grown wheatgrass cultivated indoors under artificial conditions for just 10 days produces thin, pale leaves with significantly lower nutritional content. Wheatgrass grown outdoors in its natural climate and harvested at the optimal time of year, when its nutritional value is at its peak, offers much greater health benefits. Most individuals seeking such high-quality wheatgrass opt for dehydrated powders and tablets produced by reputable companies that grow the plant organically in ideal climates, such as the Midwest of the United States and Canada. It is crucial that the wheatgrass be harvested before the jointing stage, which typically occurs for only a few days in winter wheat grown in these regions. Advocates of wheatgrass consumption claim that regular intake can boost energy levels, alkalize the body, improve digestion, prevent cancer, diabetes, and heart disease, alleviate constipation, detoxify heavy metals from the bloodstream, cleanse the liver, prevent hair loss, and ease menopause symptoms. However, these claims lack scientific validation. Dr. Samir Samman has noted that there is no scientific evidence to support claims that wheatgrass can prevent cancer, heart disease, or diabetes, detoxify heavy metals, cleanse the liver, or prevent hair loss. One of the most widely circulated claims about wheatgrass is that a single serving is as nutritionally valuable as a kilogram of green vegetables. This assertion likely stems from a statement attributed to Charles F. Schnabel, who reportedly said that fifteen pounds of wheatgrass is equivalent to 350 pounds of the choicest vegetables. While this statement appears to be an exaggeration, it was likely intended to highlight the plant's perceived extraordinary health benefits. Schnabel's research focused on wheatgrass grown outdoors in Kansas, where it underwent slow growth during the cold winter months and was harvested at a specific time in early spring, known as the jointing stage. The wheatgrass was then dehydrated and processed into powders and tablets for human consumption. This process required over 200 days of growth in Kansas's natural climate to achieve high nutritional levels. Wheatgrass grown naturally in its ideal environment develops a dense root structure and benefits from over 200 days of sunlight, resulting in a plant with exceptionally high nutritional value. Using Schnabel's research to promote wheatgrass grown rapidly in trays under artificial conditions is an invalid comparison. Wheatgrass cultivated indoors for just 10 days under unnatural conditions contains significantly less nutritional content than wheatgrass grown outdoors in climates like the Midwestern United States and Canada and harvested at the once-per-year jointing stage. Dehydrated wheatgrass powder and tablets produced from wheatgrass grown organically through the winter and harvested before the jointing stage are still available in natural food stores and online. Seven tablets (equivalent to 3.5 grams) or a teaspoon of such powder is nutritionally comparable to a USDA serving of spinach or other dark green vegetables. However, not all dehydrated wheatgrass products adhere to Schnabel's research methods. The chlorophyll molecule in wheatgrass is structurally similar to hemoglobin, leading some to believe that wheatgrass can improve blood flow, digestion, and overall detoxification. While no direct research links chlorophyll to blood-building, many nutrients found in dark green leafy vegetables are known to support healthy blood. Comparative analyses have shown that dehydrated wheatgrass powder, when grown under natural conditions, has a much higher nutritional value than fresh juice produced from wheatgrass grown under artificial conditions. Ann Wigmore encouraged her followers to dehydrate raw foods at low temperatures to preserve their nutrients. However, she misapplied Schnabel's scientific findings on dehydrated wheatgrass to support the rapid cultivation of wheatgrass under artificial conditions. In popular culture, wheatgrass has been referenced in various television shows. In the FX series Nip/Tuck, Dr. Christian Troy is shown growing and drinking wheatgrass in multiple episodes. In The Simpsons episode When You Dish Upon a Star, Homer invents a cocktail made of wheatgrass and vodka, humorously named a lawnmower. In another episode, Make Room for Lisa, Lisa is given a shot of wheatgrass juice, and her reaction to its taste is interpreted as a sign of her taste buds functioning properly. Wheatgrass is also mentioned in Sex and the City, where a character Samantha dates is advised to consume it to improve the taste of his bodily fluids.
